teaching.task: # Year 11 Chemistry M1 V15: Group 1 metals and water. Why do Group 1 metals react differently with water? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: First, safety. You won't handle these metals yourself. They react with the moisture on your skin, so they're stored under oil and never touched. In school, these reactions are shown only as a teacher demonstration, or on video. So here, we'll watch them as short video clips. Rubidium and caesium, further down the group, are never used in schools at all. Here's lithium. It's the least dense metal of all, so it floats, sitting high on the water, and it fizzes steadily as a gas is given off. It slowly moves around and gets smaller. It doesn't melt. A few drops of indicator in the water slowly turn pink around it. Now sodium. It floats too, but the reaction is faster. It melts into a shiny silver ball that races around the surface, fizzing hard. It melts because the reaction gives out heat, and sodium melts at only ninety-eight degrees. If it's held still, it can even catch fire, with a yellow-orange flame. The pink spreads much more quickly.

So here, we'll watch them as short video clips. Rubidium and caesium, further down the group, are never used in schools at all. Here's lithium. On "calmly" the trough cross-fades to `y11c-trough-li-v1.png` (steady small bubbles). On "flame" it cross-fades to `y11c-trough-k-v1.png` (lilac flame). teaching.understandingCheck: Quick prediction. Rubidium comes next in Group one, below potassium. What would happen if it touched water? Think about where its outer electron sits. Have a think. Your turn. In a teacher demonstration, equal-sized pieces of lithium and potassium are added to water. Potassium reacts much more vigorously. Explain this difference in terms of atomic structure. Pause here to answer. Last one. Two equal pieces of sodium are added to water at the same temperature. Piece A was freshly cut. Piece B had been exposed to air, and its surface is dull. Predict which piece starts reacting faster, and explain. Pause here to answer.

Status: Revision 3 (7 Nov 2026): brief 186 error check clean (root confirmed); headline count restated as the sum of scene strings. Ready to voice. Previously Revision 2 (6 Nov 2026): brief 178 review repairs applied. Needs a Codex error check before voicing. Nothing recorded; human listening pending. Voice: the Google voice (all Year 11).

Scope: fifteenth video of Year 11 Chemistry (2017 syllabus), Module 1; third periodic-trend video, after `chem-y11-m1-v13.md` (radius) and `chem-y11-m1-v14.md` (first ionisation energy, electronegativity). Templates: `phys-y11-fa1-v01.md` (structure), `bio-y11-fa1-v05.md` (plates and asset brief), `chem-m8-p02.md` (practical safety conventions), `chem-y11-m1-v10.md` (series conventions). No starter pack exists; the pack work is done here. Route entry: `chem-y11-m1-v15` in `../../programme/chem-y11-route-inputs.json` (practical: "Approved secondary footage or teacher-selected demonstration, not independent alkali-metal handling"). Site lessons read in full (5 November, read-only): `C:/Users/kygs/hscscience/subjects/chemistry/year11/module1/lesson15.sa.html` (SHA256 `421849974d14c7381b91c4e54e4a1030dc857ff9d7eddd645944bcdba744cf2c`, recomputed, matches; used: `l15-key-groups-and-their-properties-title`, its Group 1 row "react vigorously with water to form H₂ + metal hydroxide; reactivity increases down the group", the melting-point order in short answer 2) and `.../module1/lesson18.sa.html` (SHA256 `018b9247bc9bec32c086f50e45e791b0226ac4ef0dd4dab569d67bdb4b2aac36`, recomputed, matches; used: `l18-reactivity-trends-metals-and-non-metals-title`, its "metals react by losing electrons" explanation and its conditions caveat on kinetics, surface area and oxide layers; worked example 2(a), Na against K; activity 2A(a), Li against Cs). Site corrections file checked: item 4 (sodium ions are not sodium metal) is respected: the video says the metal reacts and the product contains sodium ions.

Owner rules applied: as v13 and v14, plus the practical rules: no people, hands or faces (the cutting, dropping and the teacher are never drawn; the knife and tongs are not shown; pieces appear in the trough by coded motion); apparatus and observations as painted plates, aligned, never stretched; the demonstration is stated plainly as teacher-only behind a safety screen, and rubidium and caesium are secondary sources only; "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; brief feedback with one crossed mistake; original HSC-style questions; optional key notes; Australian spelling; no em dashes; nothing in the bottom 12% of the frame.

Syllabus content (Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 1; local ledger ID `C1-IQ3-01`), quoted from `../../programme/syllabus/chem-2017-y11.json`:

- "demonstrate, explain and predict the relationships in the observable trends in the physical and chemical properties of elements in periods and groups in the periodic table, including but not limited to:"
  - "reactivity with water" (this video, for Group 1)

Source: https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/noindex/2025-03/chemistry-stage6-syllabus-word.docx (page 37)

**Boundary:** opens on v14's final frame. Teaches how the reactions are observed safely (teacher demonstration or approved footage); the observations for lithium, sodium and potassium; the shared products (hydrogen gas and a metal hydroxide solution, shown by phenolphthalein turning pink) and the word and symbol equation; the cause of the trend (each atom loses its one outer electron, which gets easier down the group, v14's ionisation energies); a prediction for rubidium and caesium (secondary sources); fair-comparison conditions; surface films (tarnish) and storage under oil, kept distinct from reactivity. Stops before a full metal activity series (Module 3), Group 2 metals, and electrode potentials (author note c).

## Decisions

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "Why do Group 1 metals react differently with water?" The answer, in order: they all make the same products (6), because each atom loses one outer electron (7); that electron is held less tightly down the group, so it is lost faster and the reaction is more vigorous (7); what you see also depends on conditions and the surface (10, 11).
- **Opening frame (equals v14's final frame).** The Group 1 first-ionisation-energy bars (Li 520, Na 496, K 419 kJ/mol) with an orange arrow "easier to lose the outer electron", `y11c-trough-water-v1.png` at the right with a "?" over the water, and the chip "Next: why do Group 1 metals react differently with water?".
- **Safety first, stated plainly (route practical; Revision 2, root decision on the brief 178 safety blocker).** Current NSW chemical-safety (CSIS) entries need a staff login and could not be verified, so the video uses the approved-video route. Scene 2: students never handle alkali metals; in school these reactions are shown only as a teacher demonstration or on video; the video shows them as illustrated clips (the aligned trough plates inside a coded clip frame). No metal size, distance or screen specification is given anywhere in learner copy. Alkali metals are stored under oil, never touched, and rubidium and caesium are never used in schools. The teacher is never pictured; the piece appears by coded motion.
- **Observations, one metal per scene (painted, aligned plates).** Lithium floats, fizzes steadily, slowly shrinks and doesn't melt. Sodium floats, melts into a silvery ball, skims about and fizzes fast; held still, it can catch fire with a yellow-orange flame. Potassium floats, melts, and the hydrogen catches fire at once with a lilac flame; it crackles and may spit. Each plate is the same trough at the same scale, so the cross-fades compare like with like. Data tags: melting points (Li 181, Na 98, K 63 °C) and densities (Li 0.53, Na 0.97, K 0.89 g/cm³), sourced (author note a).
- **One reaction, three speeds.** All three make hydrogen gas and a metal hydroxide; phenolphthalein turns pink because the hydroxide makes the water alkaline. Word equation, then 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g), with "Li" and "K" substituted on screen. Students know simple formulae and state symbols from Stage 5 and v07; the equation is shown, not balanced as a skill (balancing is Module 2).
- **Cause (site l18, linked to v14).** "Metals react by losing electrons." Each atom gives its one outer electron to water; down the group the outer electron is further out at the same core charge, so it is held less tightly (first ionisation energy 520, 496, 419 kJ/mol), lost more readily, and the reaction runs faster. Faster reaction releases heat faster: sodium and potassium melt (their melting points are low), and the heat ignites potassium's hydrogen. The video says "more vigorous" (faster, more violent), not "releases more energy overall" (author note c).
- **Prediction (3 s, scenes 8 and 9).** What would rubidium do? Answer from secondary sources: even more violent; rubidium and caesium react explosively. Their ionisation energies (403 and 376 kJ/mol) continue the trend.
- **Conditions and films distinguished (route stop).** Scene 10: a fair comparison needs the same size piece, the same water and temperature, and fresh surfaces; a bigger piece or warmer water changes what you see without changing the metal. Scene 11: alkali metals tarnish in air (a dull film forms as the surface reacts with oxygen and water vapour), so they are stored under oil; a freshly cut surface is shiny and dulls quickly; a thick film can slow the start of a reaction. The site's "oxide layer" caveat is used for Group 1 only (aluminium is named as a later example in a grey tag).
- **Memory aid:** "Further out, easier off, faster fizz." Checked in "Memory aid check".
- **Attempts (original wording, HSC style).** A1: equal-sized lithium and potassium; potassium much more vigorous; explain (3 marks). Crossed: "potassium has more electrons to give away". A2: two equal pieces of sodium, one freshly cut and one dull after exposure to air; predict which begins reacting faster and explain (2 marks). Answer: the freshly cut piece. Crossed: "the same rate, because it's the same element".
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. "Potassium reacts more because it has more electrons" (crossed in 13); "a more vigorous reaction means a different product" (6); "sodium ions in salt react with water" (6, grey tag from site correction 4); "a slow start means a less reactive metal" (11, crossed in 15).
- **Handoff (route next: `chem-y11-m1-v16`, "What do flame colours show and what can they not identify reliably?").** Scene 16: potassium's flame is lilac and sodium's yellow-orange; the colour comes from the metal, not the hydrogen. Final frame: `y11c-trough-k-v1.png` with its lilac flame ringed, `m8-flame-k-lilac-v1.png` and `m8-flame-na-yellow-v2.png` small beside it, and the chip "Next: what do flame colours show, and what can they not identify reliably?".
- **Site notes (read 5 November; for root to log in `../site-corrections-chem-y11.md` if accepted):**
  1. `l15-key-groups-and-their-properties-title`, Group 1 row: "Soft, low MP, very reactive metals" is fine, but the row gives no safety context for "react vigorously with water". Suggest adding "teacher demonstration or video only; stored under oil". Minor.
  2. `l18`, activity 2A answer (a): "Cs is far more reactive (reacts explosively with water)". Correct; suggest adding "secondary sources only" since caesium is not used in schools. Minor.
  3. `l18-reactivity-trends-metals-and-non-metals-title`: "Down a group: atomic radius ↑, IE ↓ → easier to lose electrons → more reactive." Acceptable for school level; the "more reactive" here means a faster, more vigorous reaction (author note c). No change requested.
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) the same products form for each metal (6); (2) each metal atom loses its one outer electron, which ends up making hydrogen and hydroxide (7); (3) down the group that electron is held less tightly (v14), so it is lost more readily and the reaction is faster (7); (4) faster reaction means faster heating, so the metal melts and hydrogen can ignite (7); (5) the trend predicts rubidium and caesium (8, 9); (6) size, temperature and surface films change what you see, without changing the metal's reactivity (10, 11).
- **Entry knowledge:** v12 (Group 1, one valence electron, metals); v13 (radius down a group); v14 (first ionisation energy down Group 1); Stage 5 acids and bases (indicators, alkaline solutions), word equations and simple formulae; v07 (formulae).
- **Learner-visible vocabulary:** alkali metals (the Group 1 metals, 1); hydroxide (the OH⁻ ion, which makes water alkaline, 6); phenolphthalein (an indicator that is colourless in neutral water and pink in alkaline solution, 6); vigorous (fast and violent, 7); tarnish (a dull film that forms when the metal's surface reacts with air, 11).
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Explainer motion (coded, plus plates):** **piece drop** (a small coded grey piece descends into the trough and the plate cross-fades to its reaction state; no hand, no tongs); **bubble stream** (coded bubbles rise from the piece at a rate set per metal, slow for lithium, fast for potassium; the plates carry the painted look, the motion carries the rate); **pink spread** (a coded pink tint spreads from the piece through the water on "pink"); **electron hand-off** (an inset: a Group 1 atom's outer electron leaves toward a water molecule; the speed of the hand-off increases Li, Na, K); **IE bars** (from v14); **fair-test checklist**; **tarnish wipe** (the fresh and tarnished sodium plates cross-fade on a timer); `Countdown`, `QuestionCard`, `Chip` with `cross`, `PenArrow`, scribble circle, `HandText`, `KeyNotes`, `Heading`.
- **Board layout (constant):** heading top left; the trough (inside its coded clip frame) at centre left; the data or equation panel at the right; the small Group 1 column as a locator top right.

Author notes (not learner copy):
(a) Physical data from the PubChem periodic table (retrieved 5 November 2026): melting points Li 453.65 K (180.5 °C), Na 370.95 K (97.8 °C), K 336.53 K (63.4 °C), Rb 312.46 K (39.3 °C), Cs 301.59 K (28.4 °C); densities Li 0.534, Na 0.97, K 0.89, Rb 1.53, Cs 1.93 g/cm³ (some tables give K as 0.862; both are below 1). Rubidium and caesium are denser than water and sink; not said in learner copy (secondary sources only).
(b) Observations as commonly reported for school demonstrations (for example the Royal Society of Chemistry's "Reactions of the alkali metals with water" demonstration notes): Li floats, fizzes, does not melt; Na melts into a ball and darts about, may ignite (yellow-orange flame) if held still, for example on wet filter paper; K melts and ignites at once with a lilac flame, often ending with a small crack or spit as the molten ball breaks up. The yellow-orange and lilac colours are the metal's emission in the flame (v16).
(c) Rate against extent: lithium's overall reaction with water is at least as thermodynamically favourable as potassium's (standard electrode potentials Li⁺/Li −3.04 V, K⁺/K −2.93 V, Na⁺/Na −2.71 V), yet it reacts slowest. Ionisation energy is one step of the energy cycle; hydration of the small Li⁺ ion is very favourable. Vigour (rate) follows the ease of losing the outer electron and the low melting points, which is the school-level explanation used on the site. Learner copy uses "reacts faster, more vigorously" and never claims potassium "releases more energy". Electrode potentials are Module 3 and Year 12.
(d) Equation: 2M(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2MOH(aq) + H₂(g); MOH is fully dissociated in solution (M⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)). The electron hand-off inset is a simplification of a fast multi-step process at the metal surface.
(e) Safety references for root to check against the school risk assessment: NSW Department of Education Chemical Safety in Schools; RSC demonstration notes (teacher only; safety screen; pieces no larger than about 3 mm; students at least 2 m away; face shield for the demonstrator; dispose of residues as the method directs). Revision 2 (root decision): none of these method details appear in learner copy. The video states only: teacher demonstration or video only, never touched, stored under oil, no Rb or Cs.
(f) Pronunciations: "phenolphthalein" (FEE-nol-THAY-leen); "rubidium" (roo-BID-ee-um); "caesium" (SEE-zee-um).

Main question: *Why do Group 1 metals react differently with water?*
Entry knowledge: v12 to v14; Stage 5 indicators, word equations, simple formulae.
Stops after: safe observation, Li, Na, K observations, shared products and equation, the cause, the Rb and Cs prediction, conditions and surface films. No activity series, Group 2 or electrode potentials.
Handoff: chem-y11-m1-v16, flame colours.

## Script and shots

Cue words in **bold** trigger the visual change. Colour key (continues v13 and v14): electrons blue; ionisation-energy bars orange; hydroxide pink (the indicator's colour); hydrogen bubbles white; safety items green outline; conditions checklist teal; crossed chips red strike.

- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) the same products form for each metal (6); (2) each metal atom loses its one outer electron, which ends up making hydrogen and hydroxide (7); (3) down the group that electron is held less tightly (v14), so it is lost more readily and the reaction is faster (7); (4) faster reaction means faster heating, so the metal melts and hydrogen can ignite (7); (5) the trend predicts rubidium and caesium (8, 9); (6) size, temperature and surface films change what you see, without changing the metal's reactivity (10, 11).
- **Entry knowledge:** v12 (Group 1, one valence electron, metals); v13 (radius down a group); v14 (first ionisation energy down Group 1); Stage 5 acids and bases (indicators, alkaline solutions), word equations and simple formulae; v07 (formulae).
- **Learner-visible vocabulary:** alkali metals (the Group 1 metals, 1); hydroxide (the OH⁻ ion, which makes water alkaline, 6); phenolphthalein (an indicator that is colourless in neutral water and pink in alkaline solution, 6); vigorous (fast and violent, 7); tarnish (a dull film that forms when the metal's surface reacts with air, 11).
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Explainer motion (coded, plus plates):** **piece drop** (a small coded grey piece descends into the trough and the plate cross-fades to its reaction state; no hand, no tongs); **bubble stream** (coded bubbles rise from the piece at a rate set per metal, slow for lithium, fast for potassium; the plates carry the painted look, the motion carries the rate); **pink spread** (a coded pink tint spreads from the piece through the water on "pink"); **electron hand-off** (an inset: a Group 1 atom's outer electron leaves toward a water molecule; the speed of the hand-off increases Li, Na, K); **IE bars** (from v14); **fair-test checklist**; **tarnish wipe** (the fresh and tarnished sodium plates cross-fade on a timer); `Countdown`, `QuestionCard`, `Chip` with `cross`, `PenArrow`, scribble circle, `HandText`, `KeyNotes`, `Heading`.
- **Board layout (constant):** heading top left; the trough (inside its coded clip frame) at centre left; the data or equation panel at the right; the small Group 1 column as a locator top right.

Author notes (not learner copy):
(a) Physical data from the PubChem periodic table (retrieved 5 November 2026): melting points Li 453.65 K (180.5 °C), Na 370.95 K (97.8 °C), K 336.53 K (63.4 °C), Rb 312.46 K (39.3 °C), Cs 301.59 K (28.4 °C); densities Li 0.534, Na 0.97, K 0.89, Rb 1.53, Cs 1.93 g/cm³ (some tables give K as 0.862; both are below 1). Rubidium and caesium are denser than water and sink; not said in learner copy (secondary sources only).
(b) Observations as commonly reported for school demonstrations (for example the Royal Society of Chemistry's "Reactions of the alkali metals with water" demonstration notes): Li floats, fizzes, does not melt; Na melts into a ball and darts about, may ignite (yellow-orange flame) if held still, for example on wet filter paper; K melts and ignites at once with a lilac flame, often ending with a small crack or spit as the molten ball breaks up. The yellow-orange and lilac colours are the metal's emission in the flame (v16).
(c) Rate against extent: lithium's overall reaction with water is at least as thermodynamically favourable as potassium's (standard electrode potentials Li⁺/Li −3.04 V, K⁺/K −2.93 V, Na⁺/Na −2.71 V), yet it reacts slowest. Ionisation energy is one step of the energy cycle; hydration of the small Li⁺ ion is very favourable. Vigour (rate) follows the ease of losing the outer electron and the low melting points, which is the school-level explanation used on the site. Learner copy uses "reacts faster, more vigorously" and never claims potassium "releases more energy". Electrode potentials are Module 3 and Year 12.
(d) Equation: 2M(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2MOH(aq) + H₂(g); MOH is fully dissociated in solution (M⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)). The electron hand-off inset is a simplification of a fast multi-step process at the metal surface.
(e) Safety references for root to check against the school risk assessment: NSW Department of Education Chemical Safety in Schools; RSC demonstration notes (teacher only; safety screen; pieces no larger than about 3 mm; students at least 2 m away; face shield for the demonstrator; dispose of residues as the method directs). Revision 2 (root decision): none of these method details appear in learner copy. The video states only: teacher demonstration or video only, never touched, stored under oil, no Rb or Cs.
(f) Pronunciations: "phenolphthalein" (FEE-nol-THAY-leen); "rubidium" (roo-BID-ee-um); "caesium" (SEE-zee-um).

Main question: *Why do Group 1 metals react differently with water?*
Entry knowledge: v12 to v14; Stage 5 indicators, word equations, simple formulae.
Stops after: safe observation, Li, Na, K observations, shared products and equation, the cause, the Rb and Cs prediction, conditions and surface films. No activity series, Group 2 or electrode potentials.
Handoff: chem-y11-m1-v16, flame colours.

scenes.teachingReason: Why the different speeds? In each reaction, every metal atom loses its one outer electron, and becomes a positive ion. The water takes that electron, which is what makes the hydrogen and the hydroxide. Last time, we saw that going down the group, the outer electron is further from the nucleus, with the same core charge, so it's held less tightly. Potassium gives up its electron most readily, so its reaction runs fastest. A faster reaction also heats the metal faster, so sodium and potassium melt, and potassium's hydrogen catches fire.

### 18. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
Heading on screen: "Key notes: what to write in your book".
> Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

1. Group 1 metals (alkali metals) react with water to form a metal hydroxide solution (alkaline) and hydrogen gas: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g). Teacher demonstration or video only; stored under oil.
2. Observations: Li floats and fizzes steadily; Na melts into a ball, darts about, fizzes fast; K melts and its hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame. Rb and Cs react explosively (secondary sources).
3. Reactivity increases down Group 1: each atom loses its one outer electron; down the group it is further from the nucleus at the same core charge, so it is held less tightly (lower first ionisation energy) and lost more readily.
4. Fair comparisons need the same piece size, water volume and temperature, and fresh surfaces. Tarnish (a film from reaction with air) can slow the start without changing the metal's reactivity.

Memory aid (large, on the notes screen): *Further out, easier off, faster fizz.*
